introduction: These readings hold two things together. God's essence cannot be known or described; and yet God is called Knowing, Powerful, Creator, One. The passages explain how: we know anything only by its attributes, never its essence; the names of perfection are affirmed in order to deny imperfection, not to describe; in the Essence the attributes are not distinct from it, and God was Knower before there was anything to know; the names and attributes belong to the realm of creation and are seen fully in the Manifestations, in whom alone 'personality' is found. The guide closes with passages from the Tao Te Ching, the Upanishads and Plotinus that say the same. All seventy-six quotations are read here beside seventy-six from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: 'no man hath seen God', 'naught is as his likeness', 'I AM THAT I AM', 'to whom will ye liken God', Maimonides on a unity like no other, the Shema, Paul's glass darkly, Pascal, Kant. Eight push back or add a side: Xenophanes on gods drawn in our own image, Darwin's entangled bank beside the argument from order, the Nicene Creed beside the reading on the Trinity, Spinoza twice, Aristotle's self-thinking thought, Whitman's 'be not curious about God', and Juliet asking what's in a name.
questions: If the essence of God cannot be known, what are we saying when we call God knowing, powerful or merciful?
The readings say we attribute perfections 'to deny imperfections'. How does Xenophanes's remark about oxen and horses bear on that?
'Personality is in the Manifestation.' What does this keep of a personal God, and what would Spinoza say is left?
Compare the reading on the Trinity with the words of the Nicene Creed. Where exactly do they part?
The guide ends with the Tao, the Upanishads and Plotinus. What do such agreements across traditions show, and what do they not show?
Whitman says 'be not curious about God'. Is that the conclusion of these readings, or its opposite?

outside.why: Paul exclaims: how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out.
A psalmist says of God's knowledge: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
Newton wrote that we have no idea of the substance of anything, much less of God, and know him only by his contrivances.
Paul says: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part.
Zophar asks Job: canst thou by searching find out God? It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do?
Asked his name, God answers Moses with a verb and no description: I AM THAT I AM.
A psalm names God from what creatures receive: thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.
John's Gospel says plainly, before it speaks of the Son: no man hath seen God at any time.
The Qur'an says: vision comprehendeth him not, but he comprehendeth all vision.
The Qur'an says that God's are the most beautiful names, and bids people call on him by them.
A psalm asks: who is like unto the Lord our God, who dwelleth on high?
Xenophanes said that if oxen and horses had hands, horses would paint the gods like horses and oxen like oxen. Are 'attributes of perfection' more than our own image enlarged?
A psalm says: before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
In Proverbs Wisdom says: the Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
Maimonides wrote that God is one in a manner which surpasses any unity found in the world.
Israel's confession is one line: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.
Isaiah asks: to whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
God proclaims his name to Moses in attributes: merciful and gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness and truth.
A psalm repeats the list for worshippers: the Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy.
Asked his name, the angel in Judges replies: why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?
The rider in the Apocalypse has a name written that no man knew, but he himself.
A psalm says: the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Paul says the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
Darwin contemplated an entangled bank of plants, birds and insects, all produced by laws acting around us. Does the order of nature tell us the attributes of a maker?
The Qur'an's shortest creed: say, he is God, the One; he begetteth not nor was begotten.
The Qur'an puts the rule in a few words: naught is as his likeness.
Augustine addresses God in pairs that cancel: most hidden and most near, stable yet contained of none.
Paul speaks of one dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto, whom no man hath seen, nor can see.
Whitman told mankind: be not curious about God; no array of terms can say how much I am at peace about God. Is unknowability a reason for silence, for peace, or for more words?
Isaiah names God the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy.
A psalm says of the heavens: they shall perish, but thou shalt endure.
Aristotle's first mover thinks only itself: its thinking is a thinking on thinking. Is a Knower without an object the same thought, or a different one?
God says to Moses: thou canst not see my face, for there shall no man see me, and live.
Isaiah has God say: my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
Pascal wrote that if there is a God he is infinitely incomprehensible, having neither parts nor limits.
Kant said he had to abolish knowledge to make room for belief.
Ecclesiastes advises: God is in heaven, and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few.
Job says: these are parts of his ways, but how little a portion is heard of him.
The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as God of God, Light of Light, of the substance of the Father. How does the reading's image of sun and mirror differ from that?
The Qur'an says the Messiah, son of Mary, was no other than a messenger.
Xenophanes spoke of one god, like mortals neither in form nor in thought.
The Chandogya Upanishad says that in the beginning there was that only which is, one only, without a second.
The Isha Upanishad says of the One: it stirs and it stirs not; it is far, and likewise near.
A psalm says that clouds and darkness are round about him, and justice the habitation of his throne.
Isaiah says to the God of Israel: verily thou art a God that hidest thyself.
The second commandment forbids making any likeness of any thing in heaven or earth to bow down to.
Jesus said that God is a Spirit, to be worshipped in spirit and in truth, not on one mountain.
Solomon asked at the temple: the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house?
The Qur'an says: he is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward.
Juliet asks what's in a name, since a rose by any other would smell as sweet. If the names are created, what do they tell of the one named?
Plato's Socrates calls a name an instrument of teaching and of distinguishing natures.
John's Gospel begins with the Word, through whom all things were made.
A psalm says: great is the Lord, and his greatness is unsearchable.
Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
Job, answered at last, says: I uttered that I understood not, things too wonderful for me.
The Qur'an says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth are signs for people who have sense.
Hopkins wrote that the world is charged with the grandeur of God.
Genesis says: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
Jesus told Philip: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Spinoza concluded that he who loves God cannot endeavour that God should love him in return. What is kept, and what lost, when God is placed beyond personality?
The Qur'an describes the divine will as a word: We say unto a thing, Be! and it is.
Ephesians speaks of one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.
Spinoza held that all things which are, are in God. The reading holds God manifest in all things and yet exalted above them: where is the line?
James speaks of the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
Malachi hears God say: I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye are not consumed.
A psalm asks: who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? who can shew forth all his praise?
The Levites in Nehemiah bless a name exalted above all blessing and praise.
Paul told the Athenians not to think the Godhead like gold or stone, graven by art and man's device.
Hebrews calls the Son the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person.
The first of the ten commandments is the plainest: thou shalt have no other gods before me.
The Rig Veda says: to what is One, sages give many a title.
Jesus said of the divine activity that never rests: my Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
The Qur'an calls God the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who saith unto a thing: Be! and it is.
Plotinus pictures what first proceeds from the One as light encircling the sun, generated without change in its source.
Moses reminds Israel: ye saw no manner of similitude on the day the Lord spake unto you.
Plato says the good gives to things known their being and their truth, as the sun gives sight and growth.
